'''Kathryn Ryan Cordell Thornton''' (born 17 August, 1952<ref>{{Cite web |last=Morgan |first=Melissa |date=2025-03-10 |title=Kathryn Thornton: From Alabama to Earth Orbit |url=https://southernmuseumofflight.org/kathryn-thornton-from-alabama-to-earth-orbit/ |access-date=2025-12-22 |website=Southern Museum of Flight |language=en-US}}</ref>) is an American scientist and a former [[NASA]] [[astronaut]] with over 975 hours in space, including 21 hours of extravehicular activity.<ref name="nasabio">{{cite web |author1=Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center |author1-link=Johnson Space Center |title=Kathryn C. Thornton |url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/thornton_kathryn.pdf |website=Biographical Data |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428093218/https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/thornton_kathryn.pdf |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |location=[[Houston, Texas]] |date=June 1996 |url-status=live}}</ref>  She was the associate dean for graduate programs at the [[University of Virginia]] School of Engineering and Applied Science, as well as a professor of mechanical and aerospace engineering before her retirement in 2019.  She is now Professor Emerita.<ref name=":0" />

Thornton was inducted in the [[United States Astronaut Hall of Fame]] in 2010.

== Education and organizations ==
Kathyrn Thornton graduated from [[Sidney Lanier High School]] in [[Montgomery, Alabama]]  in 1970. She later received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in [[physics]] at [[Auburn University]] in 1974. In 1977, she received an [[Master of Science]] degree in physics. In 1979, she earned a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] degree in physics at the [[University of Virginia]].<ref name="nasabio" />

== Career ==
=== Physicist ===
After Thornton earned her doctoral degree at the University of Virginia in 1979, she was awarded a [[NATO]] Postdoctoral Fellowship to continue her research at the [[Max Planck Institute for Nuclear Physics]] in [[Heidelberg, Germany]].<ref name="upi1989">{{cite web |author1=United Press International |author1-link=United Press International |title=Kathryn C. Thornton: Discovery astronaut |url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1989/11/22/Kathryn-C-Thornton-Discovery-astronaut/5006627714000/ |website=UPI Archives |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428093938/https://www.upi.com/Archives/1989/11/22/Kathryn-C-Thornton-Discovery-astronaut/5006627714000/ |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |date=November 22, 1989 |url-status=live}}</ref>

In 1980, Thornton became a physicist at the [[United States Army Foreign Science and Technology Center]] in [[Charlottesville, Virginia]].<ref name="upi1989" />

=== NASA ===
[[File:Thornton Prepares to Release Hubble Array - GPN-2000-001155.jpg|thumb|upright|Thornton prepares to release a Hubble solar array during STS-61.]]

Selected by [[NASA]] in May 1984,<ref name="PressRelease84-028">{{cite web |last1=Lawrence |first1=John |title=84-028: NASA Selects 17 Astronaut Candidates |url=https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83136main_1984.pdf |publisher=NASA |access-date=April 22, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210422133248/https://www.nasa.gov/centers/johnson/pdf/83136main_1984.pdf |archive-date=April 22, 2021 |location=Houston, Texas |pages=66–73 |date=May 23, 1984 |url-status=live}}</ref> Thornton became an astronaut in July 1985. Her technical assignments have included flight software verification in the Shuttle Avionics Integration Laboratory (SAIL), serving as a team member of the Vehicle Integration Test Team (VITT) at [[Kennedy Space Center]], and as a spacecraft communicator ([[Capsule communicator|CAPCOM]]).<ref name="rtf-bio">{{cite web |author1=Return to Flight Task Group |title=Dr. Kathryn C. Thornton |url=https://govinfo.library.unt.edu/returnflight/members/default46404640.html?id=thornton |website=CyberCemetery |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428094930/https://govinfo.library.unt.edu/returnflight/members/default46404640.html?id=thornton |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |location=[[Houston, Texas]] |url-status=live}}</ref> A veteran of four space flights, Thornton flew on [[STS-33]] in 1989, [[STS-49]] in 1992, [[STS-61]] in 1993, and [[STS-73]] in 1995. She has logged over 975 hours in space, including more than 21 hours of extravehicular activity (EVA).<ref name="nasabio" />

Thornton was a [[mission specialist]] on the crew of STS-33<ref name="sts-summary">{{cite web |last1=Legler |first1=Robert D. |last2=Bennett |first2=Floyd V. |title=Space Shuttle Missions Summary |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20110001406/downloads/20110001406.pdf |website=NTRS – NASA Technical Reports Server |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 27, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210427114154/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20110001406/downloads/20110001406.pdf |archive-date=April 27, 2021 |location=Houston, Texas |date=September 2011 |url-status=live}}</ref>{{rp|53}} which launched at night from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, on November 22, 1989, aboard the [[Space Shuttle Discovery|Space Shuttle ''Discovery'']]. The mission carried [[United States Department of Defense|Department of Defense]] payloads and other secondary payloads. After 79 orbits of the Earth, this five-day mission concluded on November 27, 1989, at [[Edwards Air Force Base]], [[California]].<ref name="MSER-STS33">{{cite web |author1=Office of Safety, Reliability, Maintainability and Quality Assurance |title=Mission safety evaluation report for STS-33: Postflight edition |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19920011290/downloads/19920011290.pdf |website=NTRS – NASA Technical Reports Server |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428095215/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19920011290/downloads/19920011290.pdf |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |location=[[Washington, DC]] |date=March 15, 1990 |url-status=live}}</ref>

On her second flight, Thornton served on the crew of STS-49, May 7 – 16, 1992, on board the maiden flight of the new [[Space Shuttle Endeavour|Space Shuttle ''Endeavour'']].<ref name=":0" /> During the mission the crew conducted the initial test flight of ''Endeavour'', performed a record four EVA's (spacewalks) to retrieve, repair and deploy the International Telecommunications Satellite ([[Intelsat]]), and to demonstrate and evaluate numerous EVA tasks to be used for the assembly of [[Space Station Freedom]]. Thornton was one of two EVA crew members who evaluated Space Station assembly techniques on the fourth EVA. STS-49 logged 213 hours in space and 141 Earth orbits prior to landing at Edwards Air Force Base, California.<ref name="ssmr-sts49">{{cite web |last1=Fricke |first1=Robert W. |title=STS-49: Space Shuttle Mission Report |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19930005547/downloads/19930005547.pdf |website=NTRS – NASA Technical Reports Server |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428100206/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19930005547/downloads/19930005547.pdf |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |location=[[Houston, Texas]] |date=July 1992 |url-status=live}}</ref>

On her third flight, Thornton was a mission specialist EVA crew member aboard the Space Shuttle ''Endeavour'' on the STS-61<ref name="sts-summary" />{{rp|88–89}} [[Hubble Space Telescope]] (HST) servicing and repair mission. STS-61 launched at night from the Kennedy Space Center, Florida, on December 2, 1993. During the 11-day flight, the HST was captured and restored to full capacity through a record five spacewalks by four astronauts, including Thornton. After having traveled 4,433,772 miles in 163 orbits of the Earth, the crew of ''Endeavour'' returned to a night landing at the Kennedy Space Center on December 13, 1993.<ref name="ssmr-sts61">{{cite web |last1=Fricke |first1=Robert W. |title=STS-61: Space Shuttle Mission Report |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19950016770/downloads/19950016770.pdf |website=NTRS – NASA Technical Reports Server |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428100614/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19950016770/downloads/19950016770.pdf |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |location=[[Houston, Texas]] |date=February 1994 |url-status=live}}</ref> Then, after [[Expedition 14]], [[Sunita Williams]] surpassed her for woman with the most spacewalks.<ref name="wrapupeva">{{cite web |last1=Kauderer |first1=Amiko |title=Spacewalkers Successfully Wrap Up Record Series |url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/expeditions/expedition14/exp14_eva8.html |website=International Space Station |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428101231/https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/expeditions/expedition14/exp14_eva8.html |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |date=February 8, 2007 |url-status=live}}</ref>

From October 20 to November 5, 1995, Thornton served aboard [[Space Shuttle Columbia|Space Shuttle ''Columbia'']] on STS-73,<ref name="sts-summary" />{{rp|105}} as the payload commander of the second [[United States Microgravity Laboratory]] mission. The mission focused on materials science, biotechnology, combustion science, the physics of fluids, and numerous scientific experiments housed in the pressurized Spacelab module. In completing her fourth space flight, Thornton orbited the Earth 256 times, traveled over 6 million miles, and logged a total of 15 days, 21 hours, 52 minutes and 21 seconds in space.<ref name="ssmr-sts73">{{cite web |last1=Fricke |first1=Robert W. |title=STS-73: Space Shuttle Mission Report |url=https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19970001426/downloads/19970001426.pdf |website=NTRS – NASA Technical Reports Server |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428101553/https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19970001426/downloads/19970001426.pdf |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |location=[[Houston, Texas]] |date=December 1995 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Thornton left NASA on August 1, 1996.<ref name="96-113">{{cite web |last1=Campion |first1=Ed |last2=Hawley |first2=Eileen |title=96-113: Astronaut Kathy Thornton to Leave NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/home/hqnews/1996/96-113.txt |website=NASA News |publisher=[[NASA]] |access-date=April 28, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428101919/https://www.nasa.gov/home/hqnews/1996/96-113.txt |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |format=TXT |date=June 5, 1996 |url-status=live}}</ref>

She was inducted into the 2010 class of the [[U.S. Astronaut Hall of Fame]].<ref name="floridatoday2010">{{cite news |last1=Best |first1=Keilani |title=Astronauts enter Hall |url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/39431358/florida-today/ |access-date=April 28, 2021 |work=[[Florida Today]] |publisher=[[Gannett]] |date=June 6, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210428102249/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/39431358/florida-today/ |archive-date=April 28, 2021 |url-status=live |via=Newspapers.com |location=[[Cocoa, Florida]]}}</ref>

=== Leadership ===
Thornton is a Director Emeritus of the Space Foundation’s Board of Directors, having joined the organization in 2010 and serving in various capacities, including as Chairwoman from 2020 to 2022.<ref name="spacefoundation">{{cite web |title=Kathryn C. Thornton, Ph.D. |url=https://www.spacefoundation.org/people/kathryn-c-thornton-ph-d/ |website=[[Space Foundation]] |access-date=May 18, 2024 |archive-date=May 18, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518190234/https://www.spacefoundation.org/people/kathryn-c-thornton-ph-d/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In November 2020, Thornton appeared at [[WomenTech Network]]'s Women in Tech Global Awards. During her appearance, she shared her experiences as a scientist and astronaut, aiming to support and inspire women in the technology sector.<ref>{{cite web |title=Kathryn Thornton - WomenTech Global Awards 2020 |url=https://www.womentech.net/video/kathryn-c-thornton-women-in-tech-global-awards-2020 |website=WomenTech Network |date=December 16, 2020 |access-date=May 18, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240518120000/https://www.womentech.net/video/kathryn-thornton-womentech-global-awards-2020 |archive-date=May 18, 2024 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Thornton is married to Stephen T. Thornton from [[Oak Ridge, Tennessee]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=A Collection of Biographies of Women Who Made a Difference in Alabama|last=Schafer|first=Elizabeth|publisher=AL: League of Women Voters of Alabama|year=1952|location=Birmingham|pages=145–152}}</ref> She has two stepsons and three daughters. On October 16, 2019, Thornton completed a through-hike of the [[Appalachian Trail]].<ref name="flv-thornton">{{cite web |title=Kathryn C. Thornton |url=https://www.firstlady.virginia.gov/womengirls/sisterhood/previous-sisterhood-spotlights/2023-sisterhood-spotlights/kathryn-c-thornton.html |website=Sisterhood Spotligt |publisher=[[First Lady of Virginia|The Office of the First Lady of Virginia]] |access-date=December 21, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231221152950/https://www.firstlady.virginia.gov/womengirls/sisterhood/previous-sisterhood-spotlights/2023-sisterhood-spotlights/kathryn-c-thornton.html |archive-date=December 21, 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>
